prompt: How does the American Heritage dictionary define imagination, as quoted in the passage?

options.text: The formation of a mental image of something that is neither perceived as real nor present to the senses
The ability to invent what has never existed before
The faculty by which the mind recalls what it has seen
The picturing of a future that God has promised

explanation: The book names its source, the American Heritage dictionary, and the author adds his own gloss: it is the art of image formation, the image of your destination.

why.a: Correct. This is the dictionary definition as quoted, including that the thing is neither real nor present to the senses.
why.b: Wrong. Invention is close to creativity in Chapter 5, but it is not this definition.
why.c: Wrong. Recall is memory, and the definition specifically covers what is NOT present to the senses.
why.d: Wrong. This is how the author APPLIES imagination, but the question asks for the dictionary definition he quotes.

prompt: What relationship does the passage draw between imagination and destination?

options.text: Your imagination sets the pace for your destination
Your destination is fixed regardless of your imagination
Imagination follows destination once God reveals it
Imagination is a distraction from your true destination

explanation: The line appears three times in the section, and it closes it: 'Your imagination sets the pace for your destination, so watch it!' Imagination is called a pace-setter.

why.a: Correct. Imagination sets the pace, which is the section's refrain.
why.b: Wrong. Genesis 13 is quoted precisely to show the opposite, that what you see is what shall be given.
why.c: Wrong. This reverses the order, and the book says until you see it, God cannot give it.
why.d: Wrong. Only NEGATIVE imagination is treated as an enemy, and even then it is to be cast down rather than ignored.

prompt: In Genesis 13:14-15, what did God tell Abram to do, and what did He promise?

options.text: To lift up his eyes and look north, south, east and west, for all the land he could see God would give to him and his seed for ever
To count the stars, for so shall his descendants be
To walk through the length and breadth of the land
To leave his country and his father's house

explanation: The four directions are named, and the moment is dated after Lot was separated from him. The lesson drawn: as far as your eyes can see is what shall be given to you, and until you see it God cannot give it.

why.a: Correct. Lifting the eyes in four directions, with the land seen becoming the land given.
why.b: Wrong. Counting the stars is a genuine Abrahamic promise from a different chapter that this book does not quote.
why.c: Wrong. Walking the land is also genuine and also not quoted here; the point turns on SEEING, not walking.
why.d: Wrong. The call to leave his country is Genesis 12 and is not used in this passage.

prompt: Which scripture is quoted for the claim that imagination is a force for accomplishment?

options.text: Genesis 11:6
Genesis 13:14-15
Genesis 1:1-3
Genesis 30:37-43

explanation: Genesis 11:6, from the tower of Babel: 'now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do.' The author's conclusion is that when imagination is set, God is committed.

why.a: Correct. Genesis 11:6 is the nothing restrained verse, and its key word is imagined.
why.b: Wrong. Genesis 13:14-15 is Abram lifting his eyes, quoted a few lines earlier for a related but distinct point.
why.c: Wrong. Genesis 1:1-3 is the creation passage used in Chapters 5 and 6 for creativity and inspiration.
why.d: Wrong. Genesis 30:37-43 is Jacob rearing the cattle he desired, cited in Chapter 6.

prompt: Which of these does the passage tell the reader to stop thinking?

options.text: Death, failure, stagnation, and lack and want because of your country's economy
Doubt, delay, distraction and division
Sickness, poverty, loneliness and shame
Fear, anxiety, concern and burden

explanation: Four commands in a row, each with its own reason: God is not a killer, failure is not your heritage, stagnation is not your lot in God, and you are not your country's economist.

why.a: Correct. These four are the ones listed, each answered with its own clause.
why.b: Wrong. Alliterative and plausible, but none of these four appear as a list in the book.
why.c: Wrong. Sickness and poverty are discussed elsewhere, but they are not this list.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the strongest trap, because fear, anxiety and concerns ARE a genuine list in the book. They are the enemies of INSPIRATION in Chapter 6, not this list.

prompt: Which pair of sayings closes the passage's charge about how to think?

options.text: Think straight and you will live straight; think high and you will live high
Think deeply and you will live wisely; think often and you will live long
Think first and you will act well; think twice and you will act once
Think clean and you will live clean; think big and you will live big

explanation: Straight and high, in that order. The parallel form is what makes it stick, and it is the positive counterpart to the four things you are told to stop thinking.

why.a: Correct. Straight then high, exactly as printed.
why.b: Wrong. Deeply and often are not the words used, though deep thinking is urged elsewhere.
why.c: Wrong. Thinking before acting is genuinely taught in Chapter 1, but this is not that sentence.
why.d: Wrong. Big sounds right for this book's ambition, but the words are straight and high.

prompt: What does the passage say most of the evils that befall people are traceable to?

options.text: The images they form in their minds
The company they have kept
Sins committed in ignorance
Curses inherited from their fathers

explanation: 'Most of the evils that befall people are traceable to the images they form in their minds.' The example given is the man who says after an accident, 'I somehow knew it was coming.'

why.a: Correct. Mental images are named as the traceable cause.
why.b: Wrong. Company shapes the mind in Chapter 7, but it is not blamed for evils here.
why.c: Wrong. Sin blocks mental excellence in Chapter 9, which is a different claim in a different chapter.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the sharpest trap, because Chapter 9 explicitly DENIES that curses have any hold on the redeemed.

prompt: Which scripture instructs the casting down of imaginations?

options.text: 2 Corinthians 10:3-5
2 Corinthians 10:12
2 Corinthians 4:3-4
2 Corinthians 3:18

explanation: 2 Corinthians 10:3-5: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds, casting down imaginations, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.

why.a: Correct. This is the casting down passage, and the book treats imaginations as strongholds.
why.b: Wrong. 2 Corinthians 10:12 is the comparison verse, used in Chapter 9 as the fifth obstacle. Same chapter of scripture, different job.
why.c: Wrong. 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 is the god of this world blinding minds, used at the start of Chapter 9.
why.d: Wrong. 2 Corinthians 3:18 is beholding as in a glass, used in Chapter 6 for meditation.

prompt: According to the passage, what specifically should be cast down?

options.text: Every negative imagination, human philosophy contrary to the truth, every negative doctor's report and story told you by your grandfather
Every doubt, every fear and every unbelieving companion
Every idol, every charm and every occult object
Every wrong desire and every impure motive

explanation: The list is unusually concrete, and the last two items are what make it quotable: a negative doctor's report and a story told you by your grandfather.

why.a: Correct. All four are named, running from the abstract to the very specific.
why.b: Wrong. Fear is an enemy of inspiration elsewhere, but this list names imaginations, philosophy, reports and stories.
why.c: Wrong. Physical objects never feature; everything cast down here is mental.
why.d: Wrong. Desires and motives are not the target; images and reports are.

prompt: How does the passage explain why certain ailments stay long in some families?

options.text: Because the devil plays around the stronghold of imagination, so the man expects the sickness at the age his father and grandfather had it
Because such families carry a genuine generational curse
Because the condition is genetically inherited
Because they have never sought medical help

explanation: The mechanism is expectation: the picture comes alive inside his mind, he does not cast it down, he does not lay hold on the truth to destroy it, so it is his turn to suffer the same ailment.

why.a: Correct. Imagination is the stronghold, and failing to cast the picture down is what completes the cycle.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the trap. Chapter 9 says outright that the redeemed cannot be cursed, molested, enchanted or bewitched.
why.c: Wrong. No physical inheritance is proposed; the book's explanation is entirely mental.
why.d: Wrong. Medical help is not part of the analysis, and doctors appear only as a source of reports to be cast down.

prompt: What rule does the passage give about positive and negative imagination?

options.text: Every positive imagination establishes a positive destination, and every negative imagination establishes a negative destination
Positive imagination pleases God, while negative imagination merely wastes time
Negative imagination can be safely ignored if it is not dwelt upon
Only spoken imagination has power to establish anything

explanation: The symmetry is the rule, and the practical conclusion follows: you must remain a man of determined imagination, constantly seeing what you desire and refusing what is of the devil.

why.a: Correct. Both directions are stated in one sentence, positive to positive and negative to negative.
why.b: Wrong. Negative imagination is far more than wasted time here; it is said to corrupt an entire destiny.
why.c: Wrong. The passage says the opposite, warning you not to think it will go on its own.
why.d: Wrong. Speech is not the condition; the image alone is treated as effective.

prompt: What reasoning does the author use when he says he cannot imagine himself in a hospital bed?

options.text: That since he cannot imagine Jesus there, and as the Father sent Jesus so Jesus sent him, he cannot imagine himself there
That sickness cannot touch a believer under any circumstance
That hospitals are a sign of unbelief
That he has been given a promise of long life

explanation: The argument runs through John 20:21, 'As the Father has sent me, even so send I you.' Because he is sent as Jesus was sent, whatever he cannot picture for Jesus he refuses to picture for himself.

why.a: Correct. The sending is the premise, and the refusal to imagine follows from it.
why.b: Wrong. He argues from identification with Christ, not from a blanket claim about sickness.
why.c: Wrong. No judgment on hospitals or on those in them is made.
why.d: Wrong. Long life is a product of wisdom in Chapter 5, but it is not the reasoning used here.

prompt: What has the author been declaring boldly for years about crashes?

options.text: "If there's a crash somewhere, don't look for me there, because I can't be there"
"No weapon formed against me shall prosper"
"I shall not die but live to declare the works of the Lord"
"The angel of the Lord encampeth round about me"

explanation: It follows directly from his refusal to imagine Jesus pulled from car wreckage while people pour water on Him shouting 'Master! Master! Are you still there?'

why.a: Correct. This is the declaration as printed, in his own words rather than a scripture.
why.b: Wrong. A real verse commonly declared, but not the sentence the book gives here.
why.c: Wrong. Also a genuine verse, also not used at this point.
why.d: Wrong. Another familiar protection verse that does not appear in this book.

prompt: Which three disciples does the author imagine coming to quell a fight between Jesus and a wife, in his illustration?

options.text: Peter, James and John
Peter, Andrew and Philip
James, John and Thomas
Peter, John and Matthew

explanation: Peter, James and John, the traditional inner three. The conclusion he draws from the picture is his long-standing declaration, 'I can't imagine me slap my wife.'

why.a: Correct. Peter, James and John are the three named.
why.b: Wrong. Andrew and Philip appear nowhere in this book; Philip appears only as the one questioning the Ethiopian eunuch.
why.c: Wrong. Thomas is never mentioned in the book.
why.d: Wrong. Matthew's gospel is cited several times but Matthew as a person is not part of this illustration.

prompt: What did Zig Ziglar say about the most powerful nation in the world?

options.text: That it isn't America after all, but imagination
That it is whichever nation reads the most
That it is the nation that fears God
That it is determination

explanation: The joke turns on the suffix: imagi-NATION. The author's application is that your imagination determines your rating in the world.

why.a: Correct. America is named and then displaced by imagination, which is the whole point of the wordplay.
why.b: Wrong. Reading is central to the book but is not part of Ziglar's line.
why.c: Wrong. The fear of God is a requirement for divine wisdom in Chapter 4, not this quotation.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the cleverest trap, because determination also ends in -nation and the book does speak of determined imagination. The word Ziglar uses is imagination.

prompt: What does the passage say about a minister who wants a big congregation?

options.text: He will never see a big congregation until he starts imagining one
He must first prove faithful with a small one
He must learn to preach before he can gather a crowd
He should plant in a city rather than a village

explanation: It is paired with a second example in the same sentence: you will never see a big business until you have a picture of one. Both restate that until you see it, God cannot give it.

why.a: Correct. Imagining the congregation is named as the precondition for seeing it.
why.b: Wrong. Faithfulness in little is a genuine biblical principle that this passage does not invoke.
why.c: Wrong. Preaching ability is not the variable discussed.
why.d: Wrong. Location never enters the argument.

prompt: What does the passage say about where many evils actually came from?

options.text: They did not come straight from the devil, but came as people gave place to the devil through careless imagination and thoughts
They came directly from the devil, who needs no invitation
They came as the consequence of hidden sin
They came through the words of those close to them

explanation: The distinction is careful. The devil is real in this book, but here he is said to gain entry through careless imagination, which is why you must jealously guard your mind against every form of negative pollution.

why.a: Correct. Not straight from the devil, but through the place people gave him by careless imagination and thoughts.
why.b: Wrong. This drops the qualification the sentence is built around.
why.c: Wrong. Sin damages mental excellence in Chapter 9, but this sentence is about imagination.
why.d: Wrong. The nearest thing is casting down a story told by your grandfather, but the cause named here is your own imagining.

prompt: What example does the passage give of people harmed by imagining trouble in advance?

options.text: Unmarried people with no medical problem who already worry they will not have children, and are first to come out when the fruit of the womb is called
Students who fear failing an examination they have prepared for
Traders who fear their goods will not sell
Believers who fear they have lost their salvation

explanation: The detail that makes it sting is that they are not married yet and have no medical or physiological problem, and yet are already too sure they will not have children easily.

why.a: Correct. This is the example given, and its force is that the trouble is entirely imagined in advance.
why.b: Wrong. A failed exam appears in Chapter 9 as a PAST failure to be forgotten, not as a fear imagined ahead.
why.c: Wrong. Business appears often but not in this illustration.
why.d: Wrong. Assurance of salvation is not discussed in the book.

prompt: Fill the blank: "Your imagination sets the {{1}} for your destination."
explanation: Pace. The book also calls imagination a pace-setter, so the word is used twice and is the one to hold.

prompt: The passage teaches that God gives what He has promised whether or not a person has first seen it in their mind.

options.text: True
False

explanation: False. 'As far as your eyes can see is what shall be given to you. Until you see it, God cannot give it.' Seeing is made the precondition, which is why Abram was told to lift up his eyes first.

why.true: Wrong. It removes the condition the Abram passage exists to establish.
why.false: Correct. Until you see it, God cannot give it, and the same rule is applied to congregations and businesses.

prompt: Where does the passage say image formation has its seat, and what does it produce?

options.text: In the mind, where ideas are turned into pictures, and these pictures create your future
In the spirit, where God plants His purposes
In the memory, where past experience is stored
In the will, where decisions are made

explanation: 'This image formation has its seat in the mind. Ideas are turned into pictures in the mind; and these pictures are what create your future.'

why.a: Correct. The mind is the seat, ideas become pictures, and the pictures create the future.
why.b: Wrong. Locating it in the spirit contradicts the book's insistence that the mind is where this work happens.
why.c: Wrong. Memory holds the past; imagination by definition deals with what is not present to the senses.
why.d: Wrong. The will is not a faculty this book uses.
